Lately, I can’t stop looking at myself in the glass of the lantern room—my reflection stares back, but it’s never right. No matter how much I lift on the old weights I keep down in the storage room, I still look small, frail—like I’m disappearing. I know, logically, that I’m not built like a boy, but in my head, I’m hollow.  

I spend hours each night under the emergency lights, inspecting my arms, my chest—digging at tiny bumps or what I think are pores or scars with a thumbnail. I’ve scabbed up both forearms so bad I started wearing long sleeves even in summer. It doesn’t fix anything, but I can’t stop.  

Yeah, I’m down most days, barely eating, don’t care about letters from my sister anymore—but it’s not just sadness. It’s that mirror. It’s the shape of me not matching who I think I should be.
